name: Wave 2 week 5: LoRA, LLM serving and cost, Dataflow and Pub/Sub, the Google PDE exam, health data privacy, clinical ML, analytics engineering and tracking plans

concepts.title: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with LoRA
concepts.kw: lora fine-tuning lora low-rank adaptation peft parameter-efficient fine-tuning qlora adapters rank alpha frozen base weights 4-bit quantisation adapter merging multi-tenant adapters trainable parameters gpu memory
concepts.s: LoRA fine-tunes a large model by freezing its weights and training two small low-rank matrices beside some layers. You train well under 1% of the parameters, on far less GPU memory, and keep each task as a small adapter file.
concepts.d: Full fine-tuning updates every weight, so a 7-billion-parameter model needs several large GPUs and each tuned copy is as big as the original. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) keeps the base weights frozen and learns an update made of two thin matrices, A and B, whose product has the shape of the original weight. The rank r, often 8 to 64, sets how much the adapter can learn, and alpha scales its effect. Adapters are usually added to the attention projections, sometimes to all linear layers. QLoRA goes further: it loads the frozen base in 4-bit precision and trains LoRA adapters on top, so a mid-sized model can be tuned on one GPU. After training you can merge the adapter into the weights, so serving adds no delay, or keep adapters separate and swap them per customer on one shared base model. LoRA changes behaviour and format well, but like any fine-tuning it is a poor way to add changing facts.
concepts.e: A team tunes a 7B model for ticket triage with LoRA at rank 16 on 8,000 examples. It trains about 0.3% of the weights on one 24 GB GPU in 3 hours, and the adapter file is about 40 MB instead of 14 GB.
concepts.c: Why does LoRA need much less GPU memory than full fine-tuning, and what does the rank control?
concepts.i: Expect to explain frozen weights and low-rank updates, rank and alpha, QLoRA, and merged versus separate adapters. Strong answers also say when LoRA is not enough and how you would evaluate the tuned model.

concepts.title: Dataflow and Pub/Sub
concepts.kw: google cloud dataflow pub/sub pubsub apache beam topic subscription pull push bigquery subscription ack deadline dead-letter topic ordering keys seek replay streaming engine exactly-once at-least-once mode windowing watermark flex templates
concepts.s: Pub/Sub is Google Cloud's managed message service: publishers send to topics and subscribers read from subscriptions. Dataflow runs Apache Beam pipelines that read those streams, transform and window them, and write results to BigQuery or storage.
concepts.d: A Pub/Sub topic can have many subscriptions, and each subscription gets every message. Subscribers pull or receive pushes, and must acknowledge each message before its ack deadline or it is delivered again, so delivery is at least once unless you turn on exactly-once delivery for a pull subscription. Ordering keys keep order for messages with the same key, dead-letter topics catch messages that keep failing, and seek replays a subscription from a snapshot or time. A BigQuery subscription writes messages straight into a table, so simple loads need no pipeline at all. Dataflow runs Beam code with autoscaling and handles event time, windows, watermarks and late data. Streaming jobs run in exactly-once mode by default; at-least-once mode costs less and has lower latency when duplicates are harmless or removed downstream. Flex Templates let others launch a packaged pipeline with parameters.
concepts.e: A delivery app publishes 6,000 rider pings a second to Pub/Sub. A BigQuery subscription lands the raw pings, while a Dataflow job computes 1-minute delivery-time windows per city, allows 2 minutes of late data and sends bad messages to a dead-letter topic.
concepts.c: Why might a Pub/Sub subscriber receive the same message twice, and how should a pipeline cope?
concepts.i: Interviewers ask how topics and subscriptions differ, how acknowledgement, ordering and dead-letter topics work, and when Dataflow is needed at all. Mention windows, watermarks and choosing exactly-once or at-least-once mode.

concepts.title: Health data privacy and consent
concepts.kw: health data privacy consent dpdp act dpdp rules 2025 data fiduciary purpose limitation abdm consent artefact de-identification pseudonymisation hipaa phi minimum necessary break-glass access audit log children parental consent
concepts.s: Health records are among the most sensitive personal data. Data teams must collect them only for a clear purpose with consent or another legal basis, limit who sees identities, de-identify data for analytics and keep a record of every access.
concepts.d: In India, health data is personal data under the DPDP Act 2023, and the DPDP Rules, notified on 14 November 2025, phase in over 18 months. Hospitals, labs and health apps act as data fiduciaries: they need consent tied to a stated purpose, must let people withdraw it, must protect data with reasonable safeguards and must report breaches to the Data Protection Board and the people affected. Children's data normally needs verifiable parental consent, with exemptions for healthcare. ABDM adds consent artefacts that say which records, for whom and for how long. In the US, HIPAA protects health information held by providers, insurers and their partners. For data teams this means separating identities from clinical data, pseudonymising IDs with a keyed hash, de-identifying extracts for research, giving the minimum data needed, using audited break-glass access for emergencies and deleting data when its purpose ends.
concepts.e: A diagnostics chain keeps names and phone numbers in a separate identity store. Analysts see 2 million lab results under keyed-hash patient IDs, age bands instead of birth dates and 3-digit PIN codes, and every look-up of a real identity is logged.
concepts.c: Why should a hospital's analytics tables use pseudonymised patient IDs instead of names, even for internal staff?
concepts.i: Expect questions on consent and purpose, de-identification versus pseudonymisation, access control and audit, and the DPDP Act or HIPAA. Give a concrete design for keeping identities apart from clinical data.

concepts.title: Analytics engineering with dbt
concepts.kw: analytics engineering analytics engineer role dbt project structure staging intermediate marts naming conventions model contracts slim ci state modified defer exposures semantic layer metricflow code review documentation
concepts.s: Analytics engineering applies software practices to the models analysts use: version control, review, tests, documentation and CI. The analytics engineer turns raw tables into trusted, well-named marts and metrics, usually with dbt.
concepts.d: The role sits between data engineering, which lands raw data, and analysis, which answers questions. A typical dbt project has three layers. Staging models clean and rename one source table each, with no joins. Intermediate models join and reshape. Marts are the facts and dimensions people query, named for the business, such as fct_orders and dim_customers. Every model has an owner, a description and tests on its keys; important marts get model contracts that fix column names and types, so a change cannot silently break a dashboard. Pull requests run slim CI, building only changed models and their children, with defer so unchanged parents come from production. Exposures record which dashboards use which models, and a semantic layer such as MetricFlow defines each metric once. dbt Labs merged with Fivetran in 2026; dbt Core stays open source.
concepts.e: An analytics engineer at a D2C brand replaces 14 copies of a revenue query in Looker with one fct_orders mart and a revenue metric. CI builds only the 6 models touched by each pull request, cutting run time from 25 minutes to 4.
concepts.c: What belongs in a staging model, and why should staging models avoid joins?
concepts.i: Interviewers ask how you would structure a dbt project, what you test, how CI works and how you keep metrics consistent. Show you think about naming, ownership and the people who use the marts.

concepts.title: Serving LLMs: latency, batching and throughput
concepts.kw: llm serving inference latency time to first token ttft inter-token latency tokens per second throughput prefill decode kv cache continuous batching pagedattention vllm prefix caching speculative decoding quantisation tensor parallelism
concepts.s: Serving an LLM is a trade between latency for each user and throughput for the whole system. The main tools are batching many requests together, managing the memory that holds past tokens, and making each generated token cheaper.
concepts.d: A request has two phases. Prefill reads the whole prompt at once and sets the time to first token (TTFT). Decode then generates one token at a time, which sets the inter-token latency and how fast text streams. Each request keeps a key-value (KV) cache of past tokens on the GPU, and that memory usually limits how many requests run together. Continuous batching adds new requests to the batch as others finish, instead of waiting for a whole batch, which raises throughput a lot. PagedAttention, used by vLLM, stores the KV cache in small blocks so little memory is wasted. Prefix caching reuses the cache for a shared system prompt. Quantising weights to 8 or 4 bits saves memory, speculative decoding lets a small draft model propose tokens the big one checks, and tensor parallelism splits a large model across GPUs. Set targets such as p95 TTFT and measure tokens per second per GPU.
concepts.e: A chat service on 4 GPUs handled 6 requests a second with static batches and a p95 time to first token of 2.8 s. Moving to vLLM with continuous batching and prefix caching for its 1,500-token system prompt raised it to 20 requests a second at 0.9 s.
concepts.c: Why does continuous batching give more throughput than waiting to fill a fixed batch of requests?
concepts.i: Senior interviews ask you to define TTFT and inter-token latency, explain the KV cache, batching and quantisation trade-offs, and size GPUs for a target load. Tie choices to a latency target.

concepts.title: Preparing for the Google Professional Data Engineer exam
concepts.kw: google cloud professional data engineer pde exam certification exam guide case study renewal exam bigquery dataflow pub/sub dataproc cloud composer storage design security practice questions
concepts.s: Google's Professional Data Engineer exam tests whether you can design, build, secure and run data systems on Google Cloud. It is scenario based: you choose the best service and design for a business need.
concepts.d: The exam guide has five sections: designing data processing systems, ingesting and processing data, storing data, preparing and using data for analysis, and maintaining and automating data workloads. Expect choices such as BigQuery versus Bigtable or Spanner, Dataflow versus Dataproc, Pub/Sub delivery and ordering, partitioning and clustering, IAM and encryption, and Composer or other schedulers. Google's page lists a 2-hour exam of 40 to 50 multiple-choice and multiple-select questions, a US$200 fee plus tax, English and Japanese, and 2 years' validity. Renewal is a shorter exam taken near the end of that period. Google recommends 3 or more years in industry, including a year on Google Cloud. Guides and case studies change over time, so read the current guide and check the exam page before booking, and treat older study notes with care.
concepts.e: A learner spends 6 weeks: two building a Pub/Sub to Dataflow to BigQuery pipeline, one on storage choices and security, one on Composer and monitoring, and two on Google's sample questions, rereading the docs for every wrong answer.
concepts.c: In the exam, how would you choose between BigQuery and Bigtable for a workload?
concepts.i: A certificate helps you pass CV filters, but interviewers then ask what you built. Pair the exam with a small Google Cloud project and be ready to explain your service choices and costs.

concepts.title: Machine learning on clinical data
concepts.kw: clinical machine learning ehr data early warning sepsis readmission prediction label leakage temporal validation patient-level split external validation calibration subgroup performance dataset shift alert fatigue medical device software
concepts.s: Machine learning on clinical data predicts things like deterioration, readmission or no-shows from patient records. The hard parts are honest labels and splits, models that still work in a different hospital, and alerts clinicians will trust.
concepts.d: Records are messy: codes vary, vital signs are irregular and missing values carry meaning, since tests are ordered only when doctors are worried. The biggest trap is leakage: a feature recorded after the outcome, such as an antibiotic order that shows sepsis was already suspected, makes a model look brilliant and useless. Build features only from data available at prediction time. Split by patient, never by row, and validate on a later period and ideally another hospital, because practice and populations differ. Report calibration and performance by age, sex and other groups, not only AUC. Choose an alert threshold with clinicians, counting alerts per ward per day, as too many cause alert fatigue. Run the model silently first, then monitor for drift. Software that guides diagnosis or treatment may count as a regulated medical device in many countries, so involve the clinical and legal teams early.
concepts.e: A readmission model scored an AUC of 0.91 until the team removed a discharge-summary flag written after the decision. Honest features gave 0.74 on the next year's patients, and a threshold of 8 alerts per ward per day was agreed with nurses.
concepts.c: Why should clinical training data be split by patient and by time rather than by random rows?
concepts.i: Expect to discuss leakage, patient-level and temporal validation, calibration, subgroup checks and alert thresholds. Interviewers like candidates who bring clinicians into the design and plan for silent trials.

concepts.title: Product event tracking plans
concepts.kw: tracking plan product analytics events naming events event taxonomy instrumentation spec event naming object action properties required types user id anonymous id identify track schema validation qa versioning owners segment protocols rudderstack amplitude
concepts.s: A tracking plan is the agreed list of product events, their properties and when each fires. It keeps app and web tracking consistent, so funnels and retention numbers can be trusted.
concepts.d: Without a plan, teams invent names like Checkout, checkout_done and orderPlaced for the same thing, and analysts spend days reconciling them. A good plan names events as object and past-tense action, such as order_completed, and lists for each one when it fires, its properties with types and allowed values, which are required, the platforms and an owner. It defines identity too: an anonymous ID before login, a user ID after, and the identify call that links them. Keep personal data such as phone numbers out of event properties. Treat the plan like a data contract: store it in version control, review changes, and validate events against it in the pipeline or a customer data platform, blocking or flagging events that do not match. Test new tracking in a staging build before release, and retire events nobody uses.
concepts.e: A quick-commerce app replaces 340 loosely named events with a plan of 60. The checkout funnel uses 5 events with required order_id and cart_value, and the pipeline flags any order_completed event missing cart_value, which fell from 9% to 0.4% of events.
concepts.c: Why should every event in a tracking plan have an owner and a list of required properties?
concepts.i: Interviewers ask how you would design events for a funnel, name them, handle identity across devices and stop tracking from breaking. Mention versioning, validation and testing before release.

concepts.title: Token economics and LLM cost control
concepts.kw: llm cost token pricing input tokens output tokens cost per request prompt caching batch api model routing smaller model max tokens context trimming semantic cache cost per user budget alerts
concepts.s: LLM costs are counted in tokens: you pay for the tokens you send and, usually at a higher rate, the tokens the model writes. Controlling cost means sending less, writing less, reusing work and using the smallest model that passes your tests.
concepts.d: Work out cost per request first: input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price, then multiply by requests a month. Long system prompts, chat history and retrieved passages often make input the biggest share, while output is priced higher per token. Main levers: trim context and retrieve fewer, better chunks; cap output length and ask for concise formats; use prompt caching, which many providers offer at a discount for a repeated prompt prefix; send work that can wait to a batch API, often around half price; route easy requests to a smaller model and only hard ones to a large one; and cache answers to repeated questions. Prices change often, so read them from the provider's page and keep them in config. Track tokens and cost per feature and per user, set budget alerts and re-check quality on an evaluation set after each saving.
concepts.e: A support bot sends 3,000 input and 400 output tokens per request, 1 million requests a month. Caching its 2,000-token system prompt, routing 70% of requests to a smaller model and capping answers at 250 tokens cut the monthly bill by about 60%.
concepts.c: Why can input tokens cost more than output tokens in total for a RAG app, even though each output token is priced higher?
concepts.i: Interviewers ask you to estimate the monthly cost of an LLM feature and cut it without hurting quality. Show the per-request formula, the levers in order and how you would measure quality after each change.

questions.q: Explain how LoRA works and why it is cheaper than full fine-tuning.

p.t: Base model weights stay frozen
Trains two small low-rank matrices
Rank sets the adapter's capacity
k: how much the adapter can learn

p.t: Far fewer trainable parameters and less GPU memory

questions.a: LoRA keeps the base model's weights frozen and learns an update made of two small low-rank matrices added beside chosen layers, usually the attention projections. The rank, often 8 to 64, sets how much the adapter can learn. Because only those matrices are trained, there are far fewer trainable parameters, often under 1%, so it needs much less GPU memory and the adapter file is tiny compared with a full copy of the model.

questions.q: You must serve a tuned model for each of 50 business customers. How would you use LoRA to keep costs down?

p.t: One shared base model with an adapter per customer
Swap or load adapters per request
QLoRA to train on less hardware
Evaluate each adapter on a held-out set
Merge an adapter only for a dedicated high-traffic customer

questions.a: I'd keep one shared base model in memory and train a LoRA adapter per customer, since each adapter is only tens of megabytes. The serving layer would swap or load adapters per request based on the customer ID, so 50 customers share the same GPUs. Training would use QLoRA, with the base in 4-bit, to fit on smaller GPUs. Each adapter must pass an evaluation on that customer's held-out set before release. For a dedicated high-traffic customer I might merge the adapter into the weights to avoid any extra latency.

questions.q: How does Pub/Sub deliver messages, and what happens if a subscriber is slow or fails?

p.t: Each subscription receives every message on its topic
Messages must be acknowledged before the ack deadline
Unacknowledged messages are redelivered, so duplicates happen
Dead-letter topics catch messages that keep failing

questions.a: Publishers send to a topic, and each subscription on that topic receives every message, so several systems can read the same stream independently. A subscriber must acknowledge each message before its ack deadline. If it is slow or crashes, the message is redelivered, so delivery is at least once and the consumer must handle duplicates, for example with an idempotent write keyed on a message ID. Messages that keep failing can be sent to a dead-letter topic after a set number of attempts, so one bad message doesn't block the rest.

questions.q: Design a Google Cloud pipeline that turns rider location events into live delivery-time metrics per city. When would you skip Dataflow?

p.t: Pub/Sub topic to collect events
Dataflow with event-time windows and watermarks
Handle late data and duplicates
Write results to BigQuery
Use a BigQuery subscription when no transformation is needed

questions.a: Riders' apps publish location events to a Pub/Sub topic. A Dataflow job reads it and groups events in one-minute event-time windows per city, with watermarks to decide when a window is complete. I'd allow a few minutes of lateness for late data and dedup on an event ID, since Pub/Sub can deliver duplicates. Results go to BigQuery for dashboards, and bad records to a dead-letter topic. If I only needed the raw events stored, I'd skip Dataflow and use a BigQuery subscription, which writes messages straight into a table with no transformation.

questions.q: A research team wants a hospital's patient data for a study. How would you prepare it safely?

p.t: Check consent or legal basis for the purpose
Give only the minimum fields needed
Remove or generalise direct identifiers
Pseudonymise IDs with a keyed hash
Control and log access to the extract

questions.a: First I'd check there is consent or another legal basis covering this research purpose, with approval from the ethics committee. I'd give only the minimum fields the study needs. Direct identifiers such as names and phone numbers are removed, and quasi-identifiers are generalised, for example birth dates into age bands and PIN codes to the first three digits. Patient IDs are pseudonymised with a keyed hash so records can be linked without revealing who they are. The extract sits in a restricted area with access control, and every access is logged, with a deletion date when the study ends.

questions.q: Design access control for a hospital data platform used by doctors, billing staff and analysts.

p.t: Role-based access with least privilege
Separate identity data from clinical data
Analysts see pseudonymised or de-identified data
Audited break-glass access for emergencies
Audit logs reviewed for unusual access

questions.a: I'd start with role-based access and least privilege: doctors see full records for their own patients, billing staff see demographics and billing codes but not clinical notes, and analysts get nothing identifiable. Identity data lives in a separate identity store, apart from clinical data, joined only through a key. Analysts query pseudonymised, de-identified tables with masked fields. For emergencies there is audited break-glass access that records who opened which record and why. Audit logs are reviewed regularly for unusual access, such as staff viewing a celebrity's or a colleague's record.

questions.q: How would you structure a dbt project for an e-commerce company?

p.t: Staging models clean one source each
Intermediate models join and reshape
Marts as facts and dimensions named for the business
Tests and documentation on every model
Owners and contracts for key marts

questions.a: I'd use three layers. Staging models clean and rename one source table each, such as stg_shopify__orders, with type casts but no joins. Intermediate models join and reshape, for example building order lines with product details. Marts are facts and dimensions named for the business, like fct_orders and dim_customers, which dashboards query. Every model has a description and tests, at least unique and not_null on keys, and the docs site shows lineage. Key marts get an owner and a model contract so their columns can't change by accident.

questions.q: Revenue on three dashboards shows three different numbers. As an analytics engineer, how do you fix it for good?

p.t: Find how each dashboard defines revenue
Agree one definition with finance
Build one mart and metric in the semantic layer
Point dashboards at it and record exposures
Tests and CI stop the definition drifting

questions.a: First I'd trace how each dashboard defines revenue: gross or net of refunds, tax included or not, order date or payment date. Then I'd agree one definition with finance and write it down. I'd build it once, in a fct_orders mart and a revenue metric in the semantic layer, for example MetricFlow. Each dashboard is repointed to that metric and recorded as an exposure, so we know who depends on it. Tests and CI on pull requests stop the definition drifting, and changes go through review.

questions.q: What is the difference between time to first token and inter-token latency, and what affects each?

p.t: TTFT is time until the first token appears
Prefill of the prompt drives TTFT
Inter-token latency is the gap between later tokens
Decode speed and batch size drive inter-token latency

questions.a: Time to first token, TTFT, is how long a user waits before the first token appears. It's driven by prefill, where the model reads the whole prompt, so a long prompt, queueing and a busy server raise it; prefix caching helps. Inter-token latency is the gap between later tokens, which sets how fast text streams. It's driven by decode, one token at a time, which depends on memory bandwidth, model size and batch size: bigger batches raise throughput but slow each user's tokens.

questions.q: Your LLM chat service misses its latency target at peak traffic. How do you improve it?

p.t: Measure TTFT, inter-token latency and queue time at p95
Use continuous batching
Manage the KV cache, for example with PagedAttention
Prefix caching for the shared system prompt
Quantise or use a smaller model, or add GPUs

questions.a: I'd first measure p95 TTFT, inter-token latency and queue time, to see whether requests wait, prefill is slow or decode is slow. Then I'd make sure the server uses continuous batching, so new requests join as others finish. KV cache memory usually limits concurrency, so a server like vLLM with PagedAttention fits more requests per GPU. Prefix caching for the shared system prompt cuts prefill work. If it's still short, I'd quantise the weights to 8 bits, route simple requests to a smaller model or add GPUs, checking quality on an evaluation set.

questions.q: For a Google Cloud data engineer exam scenario, how do you choose between BigQuery, Bigtable and Spanner?

p.t: BigQuery for analytics over large data with SQL
Bigtable for high-throughput key lookups and time series
Spanner for relational transactions at global scale
Pick by access pattern, not by data size alone

questions.a: BigQuery is for analytics: SQL over very large data, scans and aggregations, like a warehouse. Bigtable is a wide-column store for high-throughput, low latency reads and writes by row key, such as time series or IoT readings, and it has no SQL joins in the usual sense. Spanner is a relational database with strong consistency and transactions across regions, for things like global orders or ledgers. In exam scenarios I pick by access pattern: analytic queries, key lookups or transactions, not by data size alone.

questions.q: How would you prepare for the Google Professional Data Engineer exam in six weeks?

p.t: Read the current exam guide and its sections
Build a hands-on pipeline project
Cover storage choices, security and operations
Practise sample questions and review every mistake

questions.a: I'd start by reading the current exam guide and mapping its five sections to what I know. Then I'd build a hands-on project: a pipeline from Pub/Sub through Dataflow into BigQuery, scheduled with Composer. I'd spend a week on storage choices, security with IAM and encryption, and monitoring and operations. The last two weeks go on Google's sample questions and other practice question sets, rereading the docs for every wrong answer until I understand why the best option wins.

questions.q: Your hospital readmission model has an AUC of 0.92 in testing. Why might you be suspicious, and what would you check?

p.t: Look for leakage from data recorded after prediction time
Split by patient, not by row
Validate on a later time period or another hospital
Check calibration and subgroup performance

questions.a: An AUC that high is unusual for readmission, so I'd first look for leakage: features recorded after prediction time, such as notes or codes added after discharge. I'd check the split was by patient, because the same patient in train and test inflates results. Then I'd validate on a later period, and ideally another hospital, to see if it holds up. Finally I'd check calibration and subgroup performance by age, sex and ward, since a good overall AUC can hide poor results for some groups.

questions.q: How would you roll out an early-warning model for patient deterioration on hospital wards?

p.t: Run silently first and compare with outcomes
Set the alert threshold with clinicians
Limit alert volume to avoid alert fatigue
Monitor for drift and performance after launch
Involve clinical governance and regulation

questions.a: I'd run the model silently first for a few months, scoring patients without alerts and comparing with real outcomes. Then I'd set the alert threshold with clinicians, nurses and doctors, by looking at how many alerts per ward per day each threshold gives, since too many alerts cause alert fatigue and get ignored. After launch I'd monitor for drift in the inputs and in performance, and review missed cases. Clinical governance must sign off, and we'd check whether it counts as regulated medical device software.

questions.q: Design the tracking events for an app's checkout funnel.

p.t: Object-action event names in past tense
Required properties with types
Identity across anonymous and logged-in users
Validate events and test before release

questions.a: I'd use object-action names in past tense: product_viewed, cart_viewed, checkout_started, payment_submitted and order_completed. Each event lists required properties with types, such as order_id as a string and cart_value as a number in rupees, plus optional ones like coupon_code. Identity uses an anonymous ID before login and the user ID after, with an identify call linking them so the funnel doesn't break at login. Events are validated against the plan in the pipeline, and new tracking gets QA in a staging build before release.

questions.q: Product analytics events are a mess: duplicate names, missing properties and broken funnels. How do you fix it?

p.t: Audit current events and their usage
Write a tracking plan with naming rules and owners
Keep the plan in version control and review changes
Validate incoming events against the plan
Map or retire old events

questions.a: I'd start with an audit of current events: which exist, how often they fire and which dashboards use them. Then I'd write a tracking plan with naming rules, required properties and an owner for each event. The plan lives in version control and changes go through review, like a data contract. Incoming events are validated against the schema in the pipeline, and ones that don't match are flagged or blocked. Finally I'd map old event names to new ones for history and retire events nobody uses.

questions.q: Estimate the monthly cost of an LLM feature and explain what drives it.

p.t: Cost per request from input and output tokens
Output tokens usually priced higher
Multiply by request volume
Context such as history and retrieved text drives input

questions.a: I'd work out cost per request: input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price, with output tokens usually priced higher. Then multiply by volume, say 500,000 requests a month. In most apps the input side is driven by context: the system prompt, chat history and retrieved passages, which can be thousands of tokens. So a feature with 3,000 input and 300 output tokens per request costs far more from input than its short answers suggest.

questions.q: Your LLM bill doubled last month. How do you bring it down without hurting quality?

p.t: Track tokens and cost per feature and user
Trim context and cap output length
Prompt caching and batch processing
Route easy requests to a smaller model
Re-check quality on an evaluation set

questions.a: First I'd track tokens and cost per feature and per user, to find what grew; often one feature or a few heavy users. Then I'd trim context, retrieving fewer chunks and summarising old history, and cap output with max tokens. I'd turn on prompt caching for the repeated system prompt and move work that can wait, like nightly summaries, to a batch API. Easy requests get routed to a smaller model. After each change I'd re-check quality on an evaluation set so savings don't cost accuracy.
